 U1.7 Compiler construction tools

 Write a note on compiler construction tools. 5M

 Asked in: 2023-24 Final · Q7(b)


Compiler-construction tools are specialised programs that generate parts of a compiler automatically from a specification.

 1. Scanner generators (Lex, Flex): take regular expressions for tokens and produce a lexical analyzer (DFA-based).

 2. Parser generators (Yacc, Bison): take a CFG and produce a syntax analyzer (LALR parser).

 3. Syntax-directed translation engines: walk the parse tree and produce intermediate code from semantic rules attached to
 nodes.

 4. Code-generator generators: take rules that map IR operations to target instructions and produce a code generator (tree
 pattern matching).
 5. Data-flow analysis engines: gather information on how values flow through the program; core of optimization.

 6. Compiler-construction toolkits (e.g. LLVM, GCC infrastructure): integrated sets of routines for all phases.

 U2.5 Specification of tokens in detail

 What is the specification of a token? Explain it in detail. 10M

 Asked in: 2023-24 Final · Q4(a)


Tokens are specified by regular expressions. Specification needs three ideas: strings and languages, operations on languages, and
regular expressions / regular definitions.

1. Strings and languages
 Alphabet Σ: finite set of symbols, e.g. {0,1}, ASCII.
 String: finite sequence of symbols from Σ; |s| is its length; ε is the empty string.

 Terms: prefix (ban of banana), suffix (nana), substring (nan), subsequence (baan).

(i) Static allocation
 Storage for all data objects is laid out at compile time; names are bound to fixed addresses for the whole run.
 Activation records of every procedure are allocated once in the static area (FORTRAN-77 style).

 Advantages: no run-time allocation overhead; addresses known, fast access; values of locals are retained between calls.
 Limitations: size of every object must be known at compile time; no recursion (only one record per procedure); no dynamic
 data structures.

(ii) Stack allocation
 Storage is organised as a stack; an activation record is pushed when a procedure is called and popped when it returns.

 Locals are bound to fresh storage in each activation, so recursion is supported; values of locals are lost when the call ends.

 Locals are accessed as offsets from the stack/frame pointer (e.g. 12(SP) ); calling and return sequences manage the stack.
 Variable-length data (arrays sized at run time) can be placed on the stack above the fixed part of the record.

 Limitation: data cannot outlive the call that created it (dangling references if a pointer to a local escapes).

(iii) Heap allocation
 Storage is allocated and deallocated in any order from a heap area, for data that must outlive the procedure that created it
 (objects, linked lists, closures).
 Allocation by malloc/new ; deallocation explicitly ( free/delete ) or by garbage collection.

 The memory manager keeps a free list; strategies: first fit, best fit, next fit; coalescing adjacent free blocks reduces
 fragmentation.
 Limitations: slower than stack; fragmentation; memory leaks and dangling pointers with manual management.

Object-oriented languages add classes, objects, inheritance, encapsulation and dynamic dispatch. The compiler must map these
to ordinary memory layouts and calls.

1. Object layout
 An object is laid out like a record: its fields at fixed offsets known at compile time, plus a hidden pointer to the class's virtual
 method table (vtable).

 With single inheritance, a subclass layout extends the superclass layout: inherited fields keep the same offsets, new fields are
 appended. So code compiled for the superclass works on subclass objects.

 class A { int x; virtual void f(); virtual void g(); };
 class B : A { int y; void g(); /* override */ virtual void h(); };

 object of B: [ vptr | x | y ] vtable(B): [ A::f | B::g | B::h ]
 object of A: [ vptr | x ] vtable(A): [ A::f | A::g ]


2. Method calls and dynamic dispatch
 A non-virtual (static) method call is compiled as an ordinary call with the object as a hidden first parameter (this).

 A virtual call p->g() is compiled as: load vptr from the object, load the entry at g's fixed slot (index 1), call it indirectly
 passing p:

 t1 = *p // vptr
 t2 = *(t1 + 1*4) // slot of g
 param p
 call t2, 1


Because slot numbers are fixed by the class hierarchy, the right override is selected at run time in constant time.

3. Other features
 Encapsulation: access control (private/protected/public) is checked by the semantic analyzer at compile time using the class
 symbol tables; no run-time cost.
 Constructors/destructors: calls inserted automatically at object creation (heap via new, or stack) and destruction.

 Name mangling / overloading: methods with the same name but different parameter types get unique internal names, e.g.
 _ZN1B1gEv .

 Symbol tables: one per class, linked to the superclass table for inherited lookup.

 Multiple inheritance / interfaces: need multiple vptrs or itables and this-pointer adjustment.
